proposals.name: Kadovarians
proposals.entry:
Origin: Kadovar
Nature: Undead people created by the Pale Weather
Age: Every Kadovarian is at least 312 years old
Population: Finite and declining

Kadovarians are the dead citizens of Kadovar, survivors of the alchemical catastrophe known as the Pale Weather.

Every Kadovarian alive today was alive when Kadovar died.

There have been no new Kadovarians since.

Appearance

Kadovarians vary enormously.

Those who have suffered little physical damage may appear almost living at first glance.

Their skin tends toward pallor. Their bodies are cold. Their pupils commonly become dull white, giving their gaze an unmistakable quality at close range.

Older or frequently injured Kadovarians often bear visible evidence of reconstruction: stitches, mismatched skin, surgical seams, metal pins, replacement fingers, grafted limbs, anatomical patches and old battlefield repairs.

These are not necessarily considered disfigurements among Kadovarians.

A heavily stitched person may simply have had a difficult three centuries.

The Kadovarian Condition

Kadovarians are dead.

Their hearts do not function normally. They do not breathe except when forcing air through the throat for speech.

They require little or no conventional nourishment, although many continue eating and drinking from habit, pleasure or social custom.

They do not naturally heal.

A wound remains a wound until somebody repairs it.

This makes sewing an unusually important skill in Kadovar.

Mortuary Surgery

Kadovarian tissue possesses an extraordinary ability to accept replacement dead tissue.

An arm need not originally have belonged to its present owner. Neither does a hand. Or an eye. Or a section of face.

Kadovar has spent three centuries developing the medical discipline of mortuary surgery.

Simple repairs can be crude enough to perform at home. Major reconstruction requires a trained mortuary surgeon.

Kadovarian hospitals maintain Common Anatomical Reserves containing legally donated tissue and body parts for reconstruction.

Among Kadovarians, asking where somebody got a particularly good hand can be no stranger than complimenting a Fogporter's coat.

Identity

Kadovarians believe the person matters more than the flesh.

This is both philosophy and legal necessity.

A citizen might replace half their body over several centuries and remain unquestionably themselves.

But Kadovarians know there is a boundary somewhere.

Nobody knows precisely where.

Repeated reconstruction sometimes produces peculiar effects: a forgotten name, an unfamiliar gesture, a sudden preference for a food previously disliked, a dream of a house the dreamer has never visited, or the uncomfortable certainty that one's left hand remembers doing something its owner never did.

Kadovarian medicine officially regards such stories as superstition.

Kadovarians tell them anyway.

Death After Death

Kadovarians are extremely difficult to kill through ordinary injury.

They are not immortal.

Sufficient destruction of the brain can erase the continuity that makes the individual themselves.

Fire is particularly feared. Total bodily destruction leaves nothing to reconstruct.

Certain catastrophic injuries can leave a Kadovarian technically functioning but without enough intact personality to be legally considered the same person.

Kadovar calls permanent destruction the Final Death.

It is taken very seriously.

A Finite People

Kadovarians cannot reproduce themselves.

They cannot convert foreigners into Kadovarians.

The Pale Weather has never been successfully recreated—and many Kadovarians would kill to prevent anyone from trying.

There is no next generation.

There are only the people who survived the Second Morning.

Consequently every Final Death reduces the Kadovarian population permanently.

This fact sits beneath much of Kadovarian culture.

They have enormous amounts of time.

They do not have unlimited people.

Age

Every Kadovarian remembers being alive.

Even the youngest surviving Kadovarian is more than three centuries old.

This does not mean every Kadovarian is wise.

Some have spent three centuries becoming brilliant. Others have spent three centuries making essentially the same bad decisions.

Long existence has not eliminated jealousy, stupidity, greed, romance, curiosity, courage or spite.

It has simply given them considerably more time to practice.

Attitudes Toward Their Bodies

Foreigners often assume Kadovarians must be horrified by their own appearance.

Some are. Many aren't.

A stitch is a repair. A replacement limb is useful. A scar means something happened and the person remained.

Some Kadovarians carefully conceal their reconstruction. Others deliberately use contrasting thread, ornamental sutures or beautifully crafted metal braces.

Soldiers frequently leave major campaign repairs visible.

Among veterans, a body can become something of a service record.

Outside Kadovar

Kadovarians travel.

Some are merchants, diplomats, surgeons or soldiers. Others simply left.

Three centuries is a long time to remain in one's homeland.

Foreign reactions vary considerably.

Some kingdoms consider them abominations. Others consider them fascinating. Some wealthy foreigners travel to Kadovar hoping its surgeons can perform miracles upon living bodies.

And in places accustomed to monsters and stranger people, a Kadovarian may eventually become simply another neighbor.

Fogport is very good at that.

A Kadovarian living in Nine Spoons may still be called the dead girl by someone who dislikes her.

But eventually the important questions become the same ones Nine Spoons asks about anybody:

Can she be trusted?

Can she handle herself?

And whose side is she on?
